episode_title: Financial Crises: Why They Happen, How They Unfold, What to Do

stories.topic: 1929: A New York Crash That Brought Down the World
stories.summary: Through the 1920s the US Fed had been doing a poor job, and a crash on the New York Stock Exchange in 1929 triggered cascading bank failures that wiped out about 30% of the entire US banking system at the depth of the Great Depression. Within months, the impact was showing up in India. Ajay draws a direct line from that crisis through the Great Depression to Adolf Hitler and the Second World War.
stories.insight: A stock-market crash in one city ought not to topple the world economy by itself; it needs amplification mechanisms. The 'fate of the world is on the line' framing is real because financial crises are upstream of wars and revolutions, and amplification is how a local shock becomes a civilisational catastrophe.

stories.topic: 1991: The Indian Balance of Payments Crisis
stories.summary: Through the 80s, India's fiscal deficit grew, pushing up the demand for imported capital, while the country grew less creditworthy. Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait shocked remittance flows. With only 'patli gullies' (narrow alleys) of legal capital inflow because of capital controls, the system collapsed. Once everyone knew the rupee had to depreciate, exporters parked proceeds abroad, importers pre-poned dollar purchases, and Indians shipped assets out — the run amplified itself.
stories.insight: Once a depreciation becomes near-certain in everybody's head, every thinking person speculates with their own real-economy decisions, and the speculation is what makes the depreciation come true. A resilient financial system needs many institutional pathways for capital to enter and leave; monoculture is how crises happen.

stories.topic: Harshad Mehta and Bombay 1992 — Why a Bubble Is a Crisis
stories.summary: In the early 90s, Harshad Mehta extracted money from the banking system and the RBI and pumped it as extreme leverage into the Bombay Stock Exchange, creating an asset bubble that crashed. Ajay's framing of why this counts as a financial crisis: prices run the country, and when they go through a crazy boom and bust, the real sector pauses on investment in confusion. India's 1996-97 investment-boom peak should have come earlier; the BSE mess delayed the payoff from the 1991 reforms.
stories.insight: Don't anchor on bankrupt firms when defining a financial crisis — anchor on functions of finance. Prices are a public good for resource allocation; when they go haywire, the cost is felt as deferred investment across the entire economy.

stories.topic: The East Asian Crisis: Thailand's Forward-Market Trick
stories.summary: Thailand had a fixed exchange rate. When confidence fell, the Thai central bank started doing huge forward-market trades to defend the baht. One day the news broke that the bank's forward-sold position was bigger than its entire reserves — and every speculator in the world piled in to short the baht. The crisis spread to Indonesia, South Korea and beyond as speculators legitimately Bayesian-updated their beliefs about each next country.
stories.insight: The combined power of the global financial system is bigger than any government, and that is how it should be. 'Contagion' is not biological pathology — it is rational thinkers re-pricing similar risks. Markets punishing policy mistakes is a feature, not a bug, that helps keep policymakers honest.

stories.topic: The UTI / US-64 Crisis of 2000 — and a Mea Culpa
stories.summary: Around 2000, Calcutta and Bombay stock exchanges and UTI's US-64 mutual-fund scheme blew up together. Raju Chitale of MP Chitale & Sons had warned Ajay early that US-64 was profoundly wrong, and Ajay confesses he hadn't understood the depth of the problem at the time. He joined the Ministry of Finance during the resolution as a humble staffer; Bimal Jalan and S. Narayan led, and Yashwant Sinha boldly chose a 50/50 split — public money covering half the unit-holder cost and the holders bearing the other half. The assets, when later sold, netted the government's outlay back to zero, UTI was privatised, and the BSE Badla system was replaced by proper derivatives.
stories.insight: A model of what good crisis resolution looks like: net public-money cost to zero, moral hazard balanced, and a long-pending structural reform pushed through using the crisis as a window. Even an expert can be wrong on a major scientific question — admitting it openly is part of the discipline.

stories.topic: Bernanke to Friedman, On Stage in 2002
stories.summary: In a 2002 speech with Milton Friedman sitting on the same stage, Ben Bernanke (then a Fed Governor, not yet Chairman) addressed Friedman about the Great Depression: 'You are right, we did it. We are very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.' Six years later Bernanke was Chairman of the Fed when the 2008 crisis hit, and the Friedman-Bernanke knowledge framework — lender of last resort, no monetary contraction, protect the functions of finance — was rolled out at scale.
stories.insight: This is how great countries are made. Multi-generational accumulation of knowledge — Friedman and Schwartz's diagnosis, Bernanke's reasoning on financial intermediation — is then put into the hands of the same scholars when the next crisis arrives. Theory becomes practice when the thinker becomes a doer.

stories.topic: From $0.9T to $4.5T — Bernanke's 5x Fed Balance Sheet
stories.summary: Before the 2008 crisis, the US Fed's balance sheet was about $0.9 trillion. At its 2014 peak it was $4.5 trillion — five times bigger. The team of Hank Paulson (ex-Goldman, Treasury Secretary), Tim Geithner (FRBNY), Bernanke (Fed Chair) and later Larry Summers chose to do whatever it took to keep the financial system performing its functions, even letting Bear Stearns and Lehman go under. By and large the crisis was scotched within two-three years rather than dragging out as the Great Depression did.
stories.insight: It takes intellectual depth, not practical incrementalism, to go to 5x. A practitioner says 'I went 30%, that's a lot.' A thinker who has internalised the lesson of the Great Depression says 'we will do what it takes.' The decisive intervention is unimaginable without the prior decade of scholarship.

stories.topic: The 2018 ILFS Default and the NBFC Aftermath
stories.summary: ILFS blew up in 2018 not just from internal dodgy practices but as a leveraged play on Indian infrastructure development that went wrong. The crisis cascaded — Yes Bank, other firms, NBFCs and real-estate developers got sucked into the positive feedback loops. A 'private dream' of how India would do private-led financing and development of infrastructure quietly went to hell.
stories.insight: Some crises are not failures of finance per se, but leveraged plays on a deeper institutional failure — here, India's infrastructure sector. The financial crisis is the visible symptom; the iceberg below is a much bigger story about how an economy actually develops.

stories.topic: The Ila Patnaik / Ajay Shah Edge in Indian Macro
stories.summary: Ajay shares that for many years, the missing link in Indian macroeconomic discussion was that very few people deeply understood the Impossible Trinity — the Mundell-Fleming model. The unique edge that Ila Patnaik and Ajay brought to the field was that they understood it better than most others at the time, which let them again and again add value in Indian policy debates around the exchange rate and monetary policy.
stories.insight: An entire body of policy contribution can rest on deeply understanding one classical model that everyone else thinks they understand. Old economic theory, well grasped, is a sustainable competitive advantage.

core_ideas.concept: Finance Is the Brain of the Economy — and a Crisis Is When the Brain Stops Working
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's foundational definition: a financial crisis is a sudden and nonlinear impairment of the functions of finance — making prices, allocating resources, solving real-people financing problems. One firm failing isn't a crisis; even an entire industry failing isn't a crisis if alternative pathways absorb the work. The crisis is in the function, not the institution.
core_ideas.quote: We have no loyalty to finance as a means. We have a loyalty to the ends, which is — are you able to be the brain of the economy by making prices?

core_ideas.concept: Positive Feedback Loops — Why Small Shocks Become Civilisational
core_ideas.explanation: The market economy is normally a self-righting creature, but in finance more than anywhere else you encounter feedback loops that amplify rather than dampen: bad turns to worse, worse turns to even worse. A New York stock-market crash is not big enough to shake the world economy by itself; it needs to trigger something that triggers something. Tracing those amplification mechanisms is how you understand any specific crisis — and how you smell the next one.
core_ideas.quote: You've got to always watch out for positive feedback loops.

core_ideas.concept: Diversity of Pathways — A Healthy System Has No Monoculture
core_ideas.explanation: A resilient financial system has many different institutional mechanisms doing the same job, so when one fails the others absorb the work. India's 1991 crisis was made worse because there were only 'patli gullies' — narrow alleys — through which capital could legally enter. The fix is not making one channel better but having twenty channels operating in parallel. The principle generalises: design for resiliency, never rely on any single mechanism.
core_ideas.quote: When it comes to external capital flows, we should have 20 big successful institutional mechanisms through which vast sums of money come in and out of the country.

core_ideas.concept: Currency Crises and the Impossible Trinity
core_ideas.explanation: When a government tries to fix the exchange rate, the global financial system will eventually find the price the government cannot defend. The Mundell-Fleming impossible trinity says you cannot simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free capital flow, and an independent monetary policy. Soros's billion-dollar bet against the pound — and every East-Asian crisis after — is the Impossible Trinity expressing itself. The combined power of global private capital is bigger than any government, and that is how it should be.
core_ideas.quote: No government can stand up to the combined power of the global financial system, and that is the way it should be.

core_ideas.concept: Reflexivity — The World Changes Through Our Actions
core_ideas.explanation: Soros's framing for the loop where market participants' beliefs about a system change the system itself. Once five traders bet a currency will collapse, a hundred others realise their actions might actually make it collapse, and the speculation becomes self-fulfilling. Markets are not measuring an external world; they are participating in it.
core_ideas.quote: The world changes through our actions.

core_ideas.concept: The Five Categories of Financial Crisis
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's taxonomy: (1) banking crises — leveraged 19th-century-style firms holding opaque illiquid assets, hit by correlated mistakes in regulation and the business cycle; (2) currency crises — government exchange-rate management running into the Impossible Trinity; (3) debt crises — interest payments compounding faster than nominal income (private or sovereign); (4) securities-market malfunctions — the inner sanctum of finance going haywire (Harshad Mehta 1992, US-64 in 2000); (5) poly-crises that mix several together. Each has its own script; once you've lived through one, you can recognise the next.

Merton Miller's frame, expanded by Ajay: a typical Indian bank runs at 20x leverage, holds assets that are opaque (no mark-to-market price), and those assets are illiquid (no resale market). On top of this high-wire act sit correlated regulatory mistakes, exposure to the same business cycle, and toxic political-economy pressures to lend to friends of those in power. The wonder is not that banking crises happen, but that banks survive in good years at all. India's relative saving grace is that banking is becoming a smaller share of how its economy is actually financed.
core_ideas.quote: Banking is a disaster-prone 19th-century industry. — Merton Miller

core_ideas.concept: Friedman-Bernanke: Three Mistakes of the Great Depression
core_ideas.explanation: The structural diagnosis Friedman, Schwartz and Bernanke built up over decades: (1) the Fed failed at lender-of-last-resort, letting banks blow up instead of lending freely against good collateral at a penal rate (Walter Bagehot's old prescription); (2) a vast monetary contraction triggered deflation, which caused a debt crisis of its own as the real value of debts ballooned; (3) the destruction of bank-manager tacit knowledge — physical files, personal histories of borrowers — that wasn't reproducible elsewhere, choking small businesses of credit. Bernanke's career was the rolling-out of this knowledge in 2008.
core_ideas.quote: We did it. We are very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again. — Bernanke to Friedman, 2002

core_ideas.explanation: Bernanke's 2008 doctrine, applied: have no loyalty to any particular financial firm or even subsector. Bear Stearns can blow up. Lehman can blow up. What must not blow up is the functions — price-making, resource-allocation, financing solutions. The Fed's balance sheet went from $0.9T to $4.5T in pursuit of those functions, and crisis-response became a question of doing whatever it took rather than whatever was customary.

core_ideas.concept: The Standing Army for Financial Crises
core_ideas.explanation: Even with good micro-prudential regulation, a lender-of-last-resort framework, and a financial-resolution law, crises will arise that nobody designed for. Ajay's prescription is a standing intellectual army at India's Department of Economic Affairs — competent people, ready datasets, the moral and fiscal authority to convene regulators in non-rule-of-law ways. America's post-2008 Office of Financial Research is one model. You don't fight a war every day, but you keep the army.
core_ideas.quote: Finance is an unruly bubbling creature, and that's what it should be.

core_ideas.concept: Why Crises Keep Happening — Four Structural Reasons
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's four-part explanation: (1) human cognition — twenty good years teach people leverage works, and the more reckless are crowned heroes by the press; (2) bad statisticians fitting models on recent data only; (3) cleverness asymmetry — Goldman pays better than the regulator, finds chinks in any rulebook, and gets asymmetric upside; (4) state failure — bad metrics of intervention, public choice, low state capability. The conclusion is sobering: crises will always happen. Your goal is to be ready when they do.
core_ideas.quote: Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to participate in its repetition.

core_ideas.concept: Fallacy of Composition and Systemic Risk
core_ideas.explanation: What is true and safe at the level of one bank or one firm becomes false and dangerous when many do it at once. Regulators making one bank safe at a time are not making the system safe; uncoordinated moves in the same direction add up to an avalanche. Understanding systemic risk deeply is mostly about appreciating this composition fallacy — it is how individually rational behaviour produces collectively catastrophic outcomes.

core_ideas.concept: Debt Crises: When Interest Compounds Faster Than the Top Line
core_ideas.explanation: The deep intuition: borrowing from Peter to pay Paul is fine when it is principal-rolling, but when you have to borrow from Namsita to pay Vaishnav's interest, you're on a treadmill. For a country, the ratio that matters is nominal interest rate vs nominal GDP growth: when interest exceeds growth, debt-to-GDP escalates non-linearly until interest payments crowd out everything else. India hides this with financial repression — forcibly grabbing money from the banking system to lend to the government at artificial rates, which Ajay calls a violation of the Magna Carta.

Ajay's repeated theme as an Indian patriot: 1929 produced Friedman-Schwartz scholarship; that scholarship trained Bernanke; Bernanke ran the Fed when 2008 hit; the team also included a Goldman-trained Treasury Secretary and a lifetime civil servant. Multi-generation knowledge accumulation, plus bringing the best scholars into operational hot seats, is how a society makes itself capable of handling an emergency. Most countries fail at this not from any single decision but from never building the chain.
core_ideas.quote: This is how great countries are made.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's pushback: the conventional Friedman-Bernanke-Keynesian framing for both 1929 and 2008 understates the role of the state in causing the crisis to begin with. The Austrian view — Mises, Hayek, Hazlitt, contemporary work by Sowell, Shlaes, White and Kling — locates the cause in easy money under loose central banking (the Roaring Twenties; Greenspan's 2000s), amplified by state-distorted incentives (Community Reinvestment Act; Fannie/Freddie; rating-agency capture). The 2008 crisis, on this reading, was a failure of the state, not of capitalism.

core_ideas.concept: Moral Hazard and the In-Praise-of-Floods Argument
core_ideas.explanation: Amit on why bailouts that look profitable in hindsight are still wrong: they teach financial firms that reckless behaviour is insured. James C. Scott's metaphor: damming every river raises the bed until the eventual flood is far worse; suppressing every small forest fire creates the megafire that engulfs a state. Bailouts are the dam. Better to let small failures clear the system than to socialise losses into ever-bigger future crises.

Amit's fundamental objection to 'TARP turned a profit' arguments: a cost-benefit calculation must account for who bears the cost and who gets the benefit. Even if a bailout nets to zero or even profits the government, the bailout taxes the domestic help and the beggar at the traffic signal (through indirect taxes like GST) to protect the financial elite. A net-positive aggregate is not the same as a justifiable redistribution.
core_ideas.quote: The cost should not be on one section of people and the benefit to another section of people. — Suyash Rai

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing methodology: conventional wisdom shifts every era — the Great Depression has been re-read multiple times, and 2008 will be too. Default to skepticism without dismissiveness. Read the Austrians, the Keynesians, the monetarists. Don't pick a school; understand what each gets right and wrong, and reason from first principles when a new crisis arrives.
core_ideas.quote: We should always by default be skeptical of convention, not dismissive of it.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening framing: even though he addresses the audience as gentle readers, on this show he's often a gentle listener — losing count of the TIL moments while sitting opposite Ajay. His self-correction: 'If you don't agree, why are you a regular viewer? It's because of me, isn't it? I'm so hot.'

Ajay on why Amit Varma is the most loved man in the country: unlike most men, he knows how to listen. 'Every young man, learn from Amit. Learn to —' (followed by a pause that draws laughter). Ajay then adds he was going to say things to young women too 'but never mind.'
Ajay's analogy for why we ignore financial crises until they hit the headlines: 'we notice planes and civil aviation when an Air India plane crashes into a medical college hostel in Ahmedabad.'
Ajay's bedside manner for crisis recognition: 'At my age today I see financial crises the way a doctor sees a cancer. Like, you know how this is going to unfold.'

Walter Bagehot's lender-of-last-resort prescription, as Ajay translates it: only accept good collateral, lend freely, charge a penal rate — 'so people should cry when they come asking for credit from a central bank. That's the utility a central bank runs.'

On the great bank robber's classic answer: 'Why do you rob banks? Answer: because that's where the money is.' Ajay applies it to political economy — every political actor is the bank robber, banks are where the money is.

Amit's 'Incredible Trinity' bit, which he proudly debuts to Ajay: 'I owe Vaishnav 100, Vaishnav owes Namsita 100, Namsita owes me 100. Total debt 300. I borrow 100 from you, repay Vaishnav, who repays Namsita, who repays me. Total debt now 100. Actually zero — because I'm not going to fucking pay you.' Ajay's reply, deadpan: 'You think you're trying to be funny? Sorry, I am a one-track mind. When I do finance, I do it seriously.' Amit retorts: 'You just dissected a frog, but well done.'

Ajay's deadpan list of who should be in a deep liquid market: 'There should be foreigners, there should be Indians, there should be Bengalis, there should be Tamilians, there should be algorithmic traders, there should be astrology traders, all kinds of people should come together.'

Ajay catches himself sounding like a central planner: 'I hate to pick winners, I equally hate to pick losers, I hate to be a central planner — I wake up every morning dreaming that India should have a small banking system.' Amit's correction: 'You say things like we should not grow, we should do this — this we is bringing this central-planning mindset feel to it. I'm very deeply embarrassed.' Amit later adds: 'You're free to imagine your dream world, but don't use state coercion to get there.'

On Ajay's mea culpa about US-64 and M. Damodharan: 'Damodharan was right, I was wrong.' Amit immediately quips: 'So Ajay, what do you call the confession of a —' Ajay cuts him off: 'I want to tell you about financial crises. Continue.' Then: 'Continue. Okay. Strawman around.' Amit later returns to it: 'The wordsmithing that is required is what do you call the confession of a fat cat?'

Ajay's swipe at execution-only practitioners: 'You don't need to think — you know, watching these verbose mails on long-winded shows is completely a waste of time. Then those kinds of people are just there all over the landscape. They are placing bets. It's their behavior that makes the financial system.'
'Spy vs Spy' — the Mad Magazine cartoon strip Ajay invokes for the cat-and-mouse dynamic between regulators and financial-firm employees forever finding chinks in the rules.

Walter Bagehot — the 19th-century editor of The Economist whose lender-of-last-resort doctrine ('lend freely against good collateral at a penal rate') is the canonical prescription Ajay says US banking forgot in 1929.
Hyman Minsky — Amit name-checks Minsky alongside Bernanke as one of Ajay's great influences, and as one whose individual reading the GPT-5 report on financial crises explicitly summarises.

George Soros — invoked twice: as the man who broke the Bank of England in one billion-dollar day by understanding the Impossible Trinity, and for his concept of 'reflexivity' — that markets do not just measure the world but change it through their own actions.

Mundell-Fleming model — the deep macro framework behind the Impossible Trinity. Ajay credits sustained edge in Indian macro debates to him and Ila Patnaik having internalised it more deeply than most.

Robert Lucas / 'conquered the business cycle' — implicit backdrop to Ajay's contention that the 2008 response, by stabilising the economy without a Great Depression, validated decades of macro scholarship.

Veera Acharya — Ajay's friend, credited as one of the people who improved scientific understanding of the securitisation products at the heart of 2008 ('our friend Veera Acharya is an important person who participated in improving our understanding of how those products work').
Neel Kashkari — the 'Indian guy' Ajay cites as the head of the US Treasury's TARP/Troubled Asset Recovery Program whose net cost to the US government turned out to be only about $31 billion.

FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission) — the 'beautiful project' Ajay was part of, that produced the Indian Financial Code in 2015. Ten years on, only a small fraction has been implemented; Ajay calls implementation a 25-year project.

BSE Badla system — the pre-1990s leveraged-trading mechanism on the Bombay Stock Exchange that Ajay says deserved replacement; the UTI / 2000 crisis became the political window to actually replace it with derivatives, NSE clearing-corporation infrastructure, and netting-by-novation.

Yashwant Sinha's 50/50 ruling on US-64 — Ajay holds it up as a model crisis decision: half the bailout cost on public money, half on the unit-holders. When the assets were eventually sold, the public-money cost netted to zero.
Office of Financial Research (OFR) — the data-intensive standing-army organisation the US built post-2008, which Ajay holds up as a template India should emulate.
Smoot-Hawley tariffs — Amit's reference back to the EIE globalisation episode, used as evidence that protectionist state intervention deepened the post-1929 collapse.
Community Reinvestment Act / Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac — Amit's exhibits in the Austrian-flavoured indictment of 2008 as a state-distorted, not market-driven, crisis.
James C. Scott's 'In Praise of Floods' — Amit's just-published source for the dam-and-fire metaphor for moral hazard.
New Zealand's 1987 inflation targeting — Ajay's milestone for when the world finally figured out central banking. 'Conventional money took a thousand years before we got to inflation targeting.'
